summary: Defines extensions to the stateful PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) so label switched paths can be computed, activated, set up and torn down on a schedule, based on time intervals and actual resource usage in a centralized network. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some network paths are needed only at certain times, like a bus route that runs only at rush hour. This document lets a central planner reserve a path for set times and then release it.

questions: what is lsp scheduling in pcep
how to schedule label switched paths with pce
how does periodic lsp scheduling work
subtitle: How a central path computation element can book label switched paths for set times and tear them down afterwards.

tldr.problem: Paths set up in advance reserve bandwidth forever, even when no traffic uses them, so other services cannot use those resources.
tldr.mechanism: New PCEP capability bits and two TLVs carry a start time, a duration and optional repeat, grace or elastic settings, so a stateful PCE computes the path ahead of time and the LSP is signaled only when it is needed.
tldr.outcome: Network resources are reserved only for the scheduled interval and then freed. RFC 8934 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8934 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2020 and is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Schedule LSPs
sections.content:
The PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Element (PCE) compute paths for MPLS Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths (LSPs) for a Path Computation Client (PCC). A stateful PCE (RFC 8231) also knows the active paths and their reserved resources.

Pre-establishing paths from a network management system reserves resources forever, so other services cannot use them even while the path carries nothing. RFC 8413 frames the answer as scheduled reservation of TE resources: for example, a start time and duration for a bulk data replication between data centers.

This document defines the PCEP extensions for it. A scheduled LSP has a start time and a duration, and when its life ends it is deleted to free resources for other LSPs. The RFC also says the idea can apply to deterministic networks and segment routing.
sections.plainLanguage: If you book a meeting room only for the hour you need it, other people can use it the rest of the day.

sections.title: Scheduling Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC adds three pieces of state. The scheduled LSP-DB (SLSP-DB) lists scheduled LSPs. The scheduled TED is built from the TED, the LSP-DB and the SLSP-DB and shows expected resource availability now and in the future. All PCEs in the network environment MUST maintain the scheduled TED.

A basic schedule is a period from Ta to Tb. A periodic schedule repeats it: '[Ta, Tb] repeats n times with repeat cycle C' means n+1 intervals. The path is computed once for all intervals, and it may differ between repeats. If no path fits some interval, the LSP MUST NOT be set up and a PCErr is generated.

An elastic schedule, 'within -P and Q', lets the whole interval shift by X where -P <= X <= Q, and the PCE picks the shift closest to the original interval. Grace periods (Grace-Before and Grace-After) extend the LSP's life around the interval, with no resources reserved for them; the LSP carries best-effort traffic there.
sections.plainLanguage: You can book a slot once, book it every week, say it can slide a bit earlier or later, or ask to keep the room a little extra without a guarantee.

sections.title: How a Scheduled LSP Is Created and Run
sections.content:
Setup is split into two steps. First the LSP is requested or delegated and a path is obtained, but nothing is signaled. Second, the LSP is signaled at its start time.

In the PCC-initiated case, the PCC MUST delegate the LSP with a PCRpt message carrying the scheduling information. It MAY use PCReq and PCRep first. The stateful PCE checks the parameters, computes a path against the scheduled TED, sends a PCUpd with the path, and updates its SLSP-DB and scheduled TED. The PCC sees the scheduling TLV and does not signal yet.

In the PCE-initiated case, the PCE computes the path and, per local policy, either sends a PCInitiate right away carrying the scheduling TLV, or sends a normal PCInitiate (RFC 8281) at the start time without it.

At the start time, the C flag decides who acts: the PCC triggers signaling itself, or the delegated PCE sends a PCUpd with the A flag set. When the duration expires, the PCC deletes the LSP or the PCE sends a PCUpd to delete it. Changes later are sent as updated PCRpt or PCUpd messages. If a new request cannot be met, the previous LSP is unaffected and this is conveyed with an empty ERO. Synchronizing the SLSP-DB between PCEs is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: First the planner picks the road and writes it down. Only when the booked time arrives does anyone open the road, and when time is up it gets closed again.

sections.title: Capability Bits and the Scheduling TLVs
sections.content:
Support is advertised in the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV of the Open message with two new flag bits: B (LSP-SCHEDULING-CAPABILITY, bit 22) and PD (PD-LSP-CAPABILITY, bit 21). Both peers must set B for scheduling. Both must set B and PD for periodic scheduling.

Scheduling data goes in the LSP object. SCHED-LSP-ATTRIBUTE (type 49, fixed length of 16 octets) carries flags R, C, A and G, a 32-bit Start-Time, a 32-bit Duration, and two 16-bit fields that hold either Grace-Before and Grace-After or the elastic lower and upper bounds. A TLV can have a nonzero grace period or elastic range, but MUST NOT have both. A Duration of 0 MUST NOT be used, and the value SHOULD be greater than MINIMUM-DURATION, which is 5 seconds.

Flag meanings: R set means Start-Time is relative to now (clocks must be synchronized, with NTP RECOMMENDED), otherwise it is seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. C set means the PCC sets up and removes the LSP; otherwise the PCE does. A means the LSP has been activated. G means the last field holds grace periods rather than the elastic range.

SCHED-PD-LSP-ATTRIBUTE (type 50, fixed length of 20 octets) adds an Opt field, a 12-bit NR number of repeats, and a Repeat-time-length in seconds. A given LSP uses only one of the two TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: The booking form has boxes for when it starts, how long it lasts, and whether you want it to repeat. Both sides first have to say they understand the form.

sections.title: Messages and Errors
sections.content:
Existing messages carry the scheduling TLV in the LSP object. A scheduled LSP MUST be delegated to a PCE. PCRpt reports and delegates the LSP, PCUpd carries the path in the ERO (an empty ERO if no path is found) and uses the A bit for activation, PCInitiate creates it from the PCE side, and PCReq and PCRep ask for and return a scheduled path.

The extensions MUST NOT be used unless both sides set the capability bits. A speaker that gets a scheduling TLV without having advertised support MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type 19 (Invalid Operation), Error-value 15, and SHOULD ignore the TLV. A legacy implementation simply ignores the unknown TLV.

Other errors: Error-Type 6 value 16 when a scheduled TLV is missing, Error-Type 29 value 5 when constraints cannot be met for some intervals, and Error-Type 4 value 4 for an unknown Opt value. A PCC that finds the proposed parameters unacceptable reports LSP Error-value 4 (Unacceptable parameters) in a PCRpt.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sends a booking to a desk that never said it takes bookings, or forgets part of the form, the desk sends back a note saying what is wrong.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 still apply. Schedules may reveal sensitive details of network operations, and snooping PCEP messages could aid reconnaissance. A single message can instruct a PCC to set up and tear down an LSP every second for a number of times, so deployments SHOULD use PCEP security such as TCP-AO (RFC 5925) or RFC 8253, which suits sensitive information better. PCCs may also need rate limiting for scheduled LSPs.

On manageability, scheduling MUST be controlled per tunnel by the active stateful PCE. Suggested defaults are a start time one day (86,400 seconds) from now and a duration of one year (31,536,000 seconds). Implementations SHOULD let operators view scheduled LSPs and handle clock skew between PCC and PCE.
sections.plainLanguage: A schedule tells outsiders when your network is busy, so it should be sent in a locked envelope. A single order that opens and closes a road every second could cause trouble, so the receiver may limit how often it obeys.
